title: Rhythm of the Year
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart borrows a youth football coach's habit of dividing a season into phases with distinct purposes and applies it to the annual rhythm of running a school. He builds the year in three moves: transition at the end of the year, alignment at the start, and an improvement phase only once routines and relationships are established. His central claim is that September is the wrong moment to launch anything new, because staff are already carrying the cognitive load of new classes, new colleagues and new routines. Alignment, as he defines it, means rebuilding shared ways of working and trust rather than introducing initiatives, and he draws on Matthew Evans' argument that micro-interactions build culture fast enough to give whole-school change a better chance. He is candid that real years are messier than the model, but argues the phases still focus collective attention at the organisational level. The piece closes by tying the rhythm to his wider school-improvement model, in which relational trust is the precondition that protects staff from initiative fatigue.
points: The organising move is to give each phase of the year a single dominant purpose - transition, alignment, improvement - so staff know what is expected of them at each point, as players do in a phased football season.
Hart's firmest claim is a timing rule for change leaders: nothing new at the start of the year, because new initiatives compete with the cognitive load of new classes and routines.
Alignment is framed as deliberate work on existing strategies and relational trust, not as a holding pattern, and he credits Matthew Evans' 'think big, start small' argument for its payoff.
Front-loaded training and deeper problem analysis belong in the improvement phase, when staff finally have the bandwidth to implement what leaders advocate.
He treats the model as an organisational focusing device rather than a rigid calendar, admitting teams change and some individuals can improve informally at any point.
quotes: In pre-season, the focus would be on conditioning. When friendly matches began, the focus would be on practising tactical plans. When the competitive matches began, the focus would be on performance.

Alignment means, for the organisation as a whole, quickly getting back in to the swing of things, establishing routines and relationships both for children and adults, and becoming familiar with known educational strategies yet unknown children or colleagues. Each school will have ways of working, strategies for teaching core subjects, strategies for managing behaviour, or strategies for how team meetings work to name just a few.

Is the beginning of the year the time to introduce something new? I don’t think so because of the cognitive overload of asking teachers to do things better or do better things while establishing routines with new classes and getting to know new children. So when is the time to introduce new things?

We might change gears in terms of CPD and provide different opportunities for teachers who, now that they are familiar with new teams and new children, could be in a better position to actually implement any of the ideas that we are advocating.

Some colleagues might have the attentional bandwidth to be actively improving their practice at other times of the year through more informal strategies. But at organisational level, this might help to focus collective attention at different points.

Spending the first part of each year with the mantra of ‘nothing new’ whilst focusing on developing understanding, expertise and practice in existing strategies as well as building trust seems like a far better bet. Save the new things for the right time.

Maybe it stops us from introducing something new at the wrong time. Maybe it helps us to realise when we can get the best out of colleagues. Maybe it pushes us to prioritise what is certain to enable (or hinder) improvement work – trusting relationships.
